analysis.one_liner: Lets smaller derivatives dealers avoid registration as swap dealers by locking in an $8 billion exemption threshold.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Agriculture Committee, where it sat from January 2014 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, companies that deal in large amounts of derivatives called swaps have to register with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission as "swap dealers," which brings rules on margin, record-keeping, and how they treat customers. There was an exception for smaller amounts of dealing, and the CFTC had temporarily set that exception at $8 billion of dealing, with plans to revisit it. This bill would have written the $8 billion exemption into law as a floor, so that anyone dealing up to $8 billion in swaps with customers would be exempt from swap dealer registration, and the exemption could only be changed by a formal vote of the Commission. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, sent to a subcommittee in February 2014, and never moved again; it had no cosponsors and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been banks and other financial firms that deal in swaps with customers but wanted to avoid registering as swap dealers. Registration brings requirements like posting margin on uncleared swaps, keeping detailed records, and following business-conduct standards; staying exempt avoids those compliance costs. The bill would also have given those firms certainty by locking the $8 billion exemption floor into statute rather than leaving it to the CFTC to adjust.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets the de minimis quantity of swap dealing at no less than $8 billion, so an entity doing up to that much swap business with customers would be exempt from being designated as a swap dealer.

It changes the existing rule by requiring that any change to the exemption levels happen only through an affirmative vote of the CFTC, by formal rule or regulation — meaning the Commission could not simply let the level drop back down as the Dodd-Frank temporary arrangement did.

analysis.who_pays: The cost of weaker swap dealer oversight falls on the public indirectly. Registered swap dealers face margin, reporting, and conduct rules meant to reduce risk in the derivatives market; carving more firms out of registration means less of that monitoring, which leaves ordinary people and the broader economy bearing more of the risk if a derivatives dealing desk runs into trouble. Firms that do register would also face slightly less competitive disadvantage relative to exempt firms.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through thinner derivatives oversight

drawbacks.text: The bill would have locked a $8 billion floor into law, preventing the CFTC from lowering the exemption threshold as swap markets grow — over time, more dealing could escape the registration, margin, and reporting requirements that apply to registered swap dealers.

Raising the de minimis threshold to $8 billion would mean some entities dealing billions of dollars in swaps with customers face less oversight than registered dealers, which regulators and consumer advocates have warned leaves risks (such as uncollected margin) unmonitored.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is modest and concentrated: smaller or medium-sized banks get to stay below swap dealer registration if they do under $8 billion in customer-facing dealing, avoiding compliance costs. The cost falls on the public in the form of thinner oversight — fewer dealing desks required to hold margin against their bets, post every trade, and follow business-conduct rules — which was one of the safeguards Congress built after derivatives dealing spread losses through the financial system in 2008. Locking the threshold in statute would also have made it harder for the CFTC to adjust as the market grew. The bill died without action, so the cost never materialized.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee in February 2014, and the Congress ended in January 2015 without the committee ever advancing it.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Hudson introduced the bill on January 7, 2014, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.
On February 12, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management.
The bill never gained any cosponsors.
No further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, so the bill died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, existing swap dealer registration rules stayed in place, which preserves a layer of oversight on derivatives dealing — so ordinary people and regulators were better off than they would have been if it had passed. The banking industry gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Richard Hudson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it received no cosponsors and no committee action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors, and no votes were ever taken, so there is no record of how parties lined up on it.

industries.note: The bill would exempt any entity doing up to $8 billion in customer swap dealing from registering as a swap dealer, sparing them the margin, reporting, and business-conduct requirements that come with that status under Dodd-Frank. Ordinary people benefit from swap dealer oversight only indirectly — through a safer financial system — so an industry gain here runs against the public's interest in monitoring large derivatives bets.

The bill ties the CFTC's hands: it would have to use formal rulemaking, with a Commission vote, to change the exemption threshold rather than adjusting it administratively. The CFTC's authority over swap dealer designation is preserved but constrained.
